title: Raksha Bandhan (the thread)
hook: a plate with a lamp, red powder, rice, a sweet and a thread; the order you use them in is the ritual

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maha Shivaratri's pillar of light: a swan, a boar, a lying flower, and the one who said I couldn't find the end. Where did you admit an edge? Today, a thread. Day one hundred fifty.

On the full-moon morning of the month of Shravan, in the monsoon, a sister sets down a small steel plate. On it: a little oil lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few grains of rice, one sweet, and a thread. Sometimes a plain red-and-gold string, sometimes a sparkly thing the size of a coaster that her little brother will insist on wearing to school. Her brother sits facing her. Nobody needs instructions. They've done this every year since they were small. But there's an order to it, and the order is the whole ritual.
screen: `A STEEL PLATE, FIVE THINGS.` → `A SISTER, A BROTHER.` → `THE ORDER IS THE RITUAL.`

segments.voice: Here's how it goes in many homes. First the lamp is lit, and the sister circles it before her brother's face, a small arti. Then the tilak: red powder on his forehead, with a few grains of rice pressed into it. Then the thread, tied on his right wrist, with a knot or three. Then the sweet, placed in his mouth. Then his turn: a gift, and a promise to protect her. Raksha, protection. Bandhan, a bond. Now, the stories. On this path you've heard the one about Draupadi binding Krishna's cut finger. There's an older one, in the Bhavishya Purana. The gods are losing a war with the demons, and the wife of Indra, king of the gods, ties a protective thread on his wrist before battle, and he wins. Notice: there, it's a wife protecting her husband, not a sister. The thread was protection before it was about siblings. And the same full moon holds other threads too. In many South Indian families, men who wear the sacred thread across the chest change it for a new one that morning, a day called Avani Avittam. On the coast of Maharashtra, fishing families offer coconuts to the sea, asking it to be gentle for the season. So Raksha Bandhan isn't really one custom. It's a full moon when people tie things: to each other, to the sea, to their own promises. Today, many sisters tie rakhis on sisters, cousins tie them on cousins, friends on friends, and some people tie one on a tree they've promised to look after. Protection turns out to run in every direction.
screen: `LAMP, TILAK, THREAD, SWEET, PROMISE.` · `INDRA'S WIFE TIES THE FIRST THREAD.` · `ONE FULL MOON, MANY THREADS.` · `PROTECTION RUNS EVERY DIRECTION.` · then, large: `RAKSHA, PROTECTION. BANDHAN, A BOND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tie a thread in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you'd protect without being asked. A sibling, a friend, a child, an old neighbor. Picture the plate. Light the little lamp and circle it once before their face. Touch their forehead. Tie the thread on their wrist, one knot, and as you pull it snug, notice what you're promising. Then the sweet. Now turn it around: who would tie one on you? Let yourself be the one protected for a breath or two. The bell holds the time.
Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection, tied on the full moon of Shravan with a lamp, a tilak, a thread and a sweet.
Your line: Raksha Bandhan, the thread. Today, tell one person, plainly, that you've got their back. Then keep it. Day one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravan, many Hindu sisters perform a small arti for their brothers, apply a tilak, tie a rakhi on the wrist and feed them a sweet, and brothers give a gift and a promise of protection; today rakhis are also tied between sisters, cousins and friends.

original.note: Sanskrit: raksha, protection, and bandhana, a tie or bond.

trapdoor: what it means: a full moon for tying protection: lamp, tilak, thread, sweet and a promise, in more directions than one.
what a scholar hears: the Bhavishya Purana's thread tied by Indra's wife, and the same full moon's Avani Avittam and coconut offerings.

sources.ref: Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva (Indrani ties a raksha on Indra)
Raksha Bandhan observance; Avani Avittam (upakarma); Narali Purnima

notes: Indrani (Shachi) tying a raksha on Indra: Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva 137. Confirm the reference.
Order of the ritual (arti, tilak with akshat, rakhi on right wrist, sweet, gift and promise): common but varies by family. Confirm.

Avani Avittam/upakarma: renewal of the yajnopavita on Shravan Purnima (for Rig and Yajur Vedins), mainly among communities who wear it. Written as 'in many South Indian families, men who wear the sacred thread'. Confirm.
Narali Purnima coconut offering by coastal (Koli) communities in Maharashtra. Confirm.
Tying rakhis on trees (vriksha bandhan): a modern practice. Confirm.
